tour.title: The Philosopher's Path & Northern Zen
tour.summary: A slow winter morning south through Kyoto's temple hills — a shogun's silver-less pavilion, a philosopher's canal lane, a thatched Pure Land gate, a looking-back Buddha, the aqueduct at the top of Zen, and the shrine that re-invented Kyoto's imperial past.
tour.overviewText:
Kyoto in late January is a city with the crowds switched off. The tour buses thin out, the maples are bare sticks, and the temples stand in cold blue light with almost nobody in them — which is exactly why this is the week to walk the north-east of the city on foot. What you are walking through is not scenery. It is the workshop where a large part of what the world now calls Japanese taste was invented, and much of it is still standing.

Kyoto was Japan's capital for more than a thousand years. Emperor Kanmu founded it in 794 as Heian-kyō, "capital of peace and tranquillity", laid out on a Chinese grid borrowed from Chang'an, the Tang dynasty capital. The court ruled from here until 1868, when the Meiji government moved the emperor to Tokyo — a rupture that cut the city's population by roughly a third and left it to invent a new reason to exist. It kept the temples, and eventually it learned to live off them.

The aesthetic you are here for was born from catastrophe. In the fifteenth century the shogun — the hereditary military ruler who governed in the emperor's name — was Ashikaga Yoshimasa, eighth of the Ashikaga line. He was a poor politician. His failure to settle his own succession helped trigger the Ōnin War of 1467 to 1477, a decade of street fighting that burned much of Kyoto and opened a century of civil war. In 1473 he stopped even pretending to govern, retired to the eastern hills, and spent his last years building a villa and filling it with poets, painters and tea masters. That circle produced what is called Higashiyama culture — the tea ceremony, Noh theatre, flower arranging, ink painting, and the taste known as wabi-sabi, which finds beauty in what is plain, old and imperfect.

Two faiths share this ground, and today you cross both. Buddhism reached Japan from the mainland in the sixth century and split into schools that still compete: Rinzai Zen, the austere meditation school favoured by the warrior elite, and Jōdo, the Pure Land school, which taught that ordinary people could be saved by faith alone. Shinto, Japan's older religion, is a faith of places, marking the spots where a kami — a spirit or deity — is felt to be present. Most Japanese families use both without contradiction, and you will.

The walk is a slow line south through the Higashiyama foothills. It starts at the great Zen villa in the north, follows the canal-side lane that a philosopher made famous, detours to two quieter temples, and finishes among the Meiji-era pageantry of a shrine built to prove Kyoto still mattered.

Late January and early February are ideal but cold, and the days are short: the temples here close between 16:30 and 17:00, so start in the morning. Bring coins — several of these gates take cash only and sell no online tickets — and expect a handful of fees. The lane itself and the shrine grounds are free.

Walk it slowly, in one direction, and let the emptiness do the work.
tour.difficulty: Easy to moderate. Mostly gentle downhill on paved lanes and stone paths, but there are steps at almost every temple — Ginkaku-ji's garden is a stepped one-way loop, Hōnen-in's gate and grounds are uneven, Eikan-dō climbs a hillside on wooden walkways, and Nanzen-ji's Sanmon staircase is very steep. The Philosopher's Path and Heian Shrine's courtyard are the level stretches.
tour.bestTimeOfDay: Start at Ginkaku-ji at opening — 9:00 in winter — and walk south through the morning. The temples in this part of Kyoto close by 16:30 to 17:00 in late January and early February, so a late-afternoon start will not fit them all in. Aim to reach Nanzen-ji by about 14:00 and Heian Shrine before dusk, around 17:00. Weekday mornings are quietest; the Philosopher's Path is at its emptiest before 10:00.
tour.imageCredits: Photographs are bundled from Wikimedia Commons under public domain or Creative Commons licences. Full attribution for each image appears on its stop page and in Settings.

stops.name: Ginkaku-ji (the Silver Pavilion)
stops.narration:
You are looking at the most famous piece of silver in Japan, and there is no silver on it. The Kannon-den — the two-storey hall in front of you, dark weathered wood under a pyramid of shingles — has never carried a sheet of silver leaf. The usual story is that the shogun Ashikaga Yoshimasa meant to coat it in silver to answer his grandfather's Golden Pavilion across town, ran short of money, and left it bare; the temple's own account is vaguer, saying the nickname probably arrived generations later, in the Edo period, as a pointed contrast to the gold. Either way, the bare wood is the point.

Meet the man. Yoshimasa was the eighth shogun of the Ashikaga shogunate, the military government that ran Japan from this city in the Muromachi period. He became shogun at thirteen in 1449, presided over the Ōnin War — a decade of street fighting from 1467 that burned much of Kyoto to the ground and opened a century of civil war — and then, in 1473, handed the title to his young son and walked away from politics to build a retirement villa in the eastern hills. Construction began in 1482. Yoshimasa died in 1490, a year after the pavilion was finished, and by his own wish the villa became a Zen temple, Jishō-ji.

What he built instead of an empire is Higashiyama culture — the cluster of arts that formed around his salon: the tea ceremony, Noh theatre, flower arranging, ink painting, and the taste later named wabi-sabi. Wabi is the beauty of the plain and the quiet; sabi is the beauty of age and wear. Hold that and the garden in front of you makes sense: moss, unpolished timber, a pond and a hillside, no gilding.

Two details repay a minute each. The Tōgudō, the smaller hall on one side and a National Treasure, contains a four-and-a-half-mat room called the Dōjinsai — Yoshimasa's study, with a built-in desk and staggered shelves, and the oldest surviving room of its kind. It is an ancestor of the tearoom; tea masters and their patrons copied its proportions for centuries. And in the garden the two pale sand works — the Ginshadan, raked into long wave-lines, and the Kōgetsudai, the flat-topped cone beside it — are not medieval at all; they date from the Edo period, and the pretty story that they were built to throw moonlight onto the pavilion is folklore, not record.

Practicalities: admission was ¥1,000 for adults and ¥500 for children from 1 April 2026 — the first rise in 32 years, and most guidebooks still print the old price — so carry cash and verify at the gate. In winter, December to February, it opens at 9:00 and closes at 16:30, and the route is a one-way loop, so there is no turning back. Take it slowly.
stops.entranceFeeNote: Around ¥1,000 for high-school age and above and ¥500 for elementary and junior-high children since 1 April 2026, when the fee doubled for the first time in 32 years. Cash at the gate only — there is no online or advance ticket. Prices change, so verify at the gate.
stops.openingHours: Open daily, no closing days. 8:30 to 17:00 from March to November, and 9:00 to 16:30 from December to the end of February — the winter closing time catches people out. Confirm at the gate.
stops.accessibility: Not step-free, honestly. The visit is a one-way circuit with a stepped climb up the hillside garden and back down; there are wooden steps and uneven moss-and-gravel paths throughout. The flat area is limited to the entrance and the sand garden viewpoint.
stops.insiderTip: Walk straight up to the hillside viewpoint first, before the pavilion — from up there the whole composition of pond, moss and roofs reads at once, and you descend into the garden with it in your head. Ask at the gate whether the Tōgudō's Dōjinsai room is viewable; it is usually closed, but it is the real treasure here.
stops.nextStopDirections: Leave Ginkaku-ji by the exit and walk south: the lane in front of the temple becomes the northern end of the Philosopher's Path within a couple of minutes. Follow the canal-side lane downhill, past the first small shops, and stop where the path runs straight with the water on your left — that is the next stop, roughly half a kilometre along.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: Cun Cun, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

stops.name: The Philosopher's Path
stops.narration:
A philosopher walked this lane, and the city eventually renamed it after him. His name was Nishida Kitarō (1870–1945), a professor of philosophy at Kyoto Imperial University, and from about 1910 until he retired in 1928 he walked this canal-side path almost daily — his biographer describes outings of two hours or more — on the way to and from the university. He was the founder of what is called the Kyoto School: a group of Japanese thinkers who spent the twentieth century trying to put Western philosophy — Kant, Hegel, Heidegger — into a real conversation with Zen and Buddhist thought. The name Tetsugaku no Michi, Philosopher's Path, was made official only in the 1970s, when residents fighting to protect the lane as a walking path settled on it.

The lane is a canal bank, and the canal is the interesting part. This is a branch of the Lake Biwa Canal, completed in 1890 by engineers who dug and tunnelled over the mountains to bring water roughly eleven kilometres from Lake Biwa, in the next prefecture, into Kyoto. Read that as an act of survival. The emperor and the court had left for Tokyo in 1868, and Kyoto — capital for more than a thousand years — lost a third of its people and its reason to exist. The canal gave the city drinking water, irrigated the fields, floated freight, and from 1891 powered Japan's first commercial hydroelectric plant, which in turn ran the country's first electric tram. You are standing on a side effect of industrial policy: a maintenance road that became one of Japan's hundred best paths.

The cherry trees are a gift with a name. In 1921 the Kyoto painter Hashimoto Kansetsu and his wife Yone donated three hundred Somei-Yoshino saplings, planted along this stretch; another hundred and fifty followed in 1932, as thanks for what the city had given the artist. Somei-Yoshino are short-lived, and most of the originals have been replaced, but around 430 cherry trees now line the path — bare sticks in the week you are walking, which is exactly why you can see the canal, the houses and the hillsides properly. In early April this same lane carries crowds that are hard to believe.

Walk slowly and you will notice two things most people miss. First, a stone memorial to Nishida set into one corner, inscribed with a line usually translated as "You are you, and I am I" — an oddly individualist sentiment for a philosopher steeped in Buddhist thought about the self dissolving. Second, the path is genuinely residential: houses and small shops open straight onto it, and the cats sunning themselves here belong to a neighbourhood, not to you. Keep your voice down and stay out of people's doorways.

It is free and open at any hour — a stone lane with gentle slopes and no steps. It runs about two kilometres from Ginkaku-ji down to Nanzen-ji; we join it here and leave it for the temple detour ahead.
stops.entranceFeeNote: Free public lane, open at all hours. Small cafés and shops along it charge their own prices.
stops.openingHours: Open at all hours, free. Quietest before 10:00. It is a working residential lane, so keep voices low and do not block doorways or driveways.
stops.accessibility: Mostly level stone path with a few gentle slopes and short flights where it meets side streets. No steps along the main canal stretch between Ginkaku-ji and the Nanzen-ji area, but the surface is uneven and can be slippery after rain.
stops.insiderTip: Look for the small stone memorial to Nishida Kitarō set into one corner of the path — most walkers pass it without noticing. In winter, without the blossom, you can actually see the canal and the old neighbourhood behind the trees; in spring the same lane is a shoulder-to-shoulder procession.
stops.nextStopDirections: Continue south along the path for a few minutes until you reach a signed turn to the left for Hōnen-in. Leave the canal, walk a short way uphill into the quiet residential lane, and the thatched gate is at the end of it — Hōnen-in sits a minute or two off the path.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: shankar s., CC BY 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons

stops.name: Honen-in
stops.narration:
Stop at the gate before you go in. That low, heavy thatched roof — moss creeping up the straw, ferns in the corners, the whole thing reading more like a farmhouse than a temple entrance — is the reason people come. It is built in sukiya-zukuri, the tea-house style: deliberately rustic, deliberately unmonumental. A gate like this announces that you are leaving the loud world behind.

Two raised beds of white sand sit just inside, their tops raked into patterns that change with the season; walking between them is meant as purification, so pass through rather than around. On the old stone marker at the gate you can still make out a rule of the stricter Buddhist life: no garlic, no meat, no alcohol beyond this point.

Now the history, because it is a story about who religion was for. This was the site of the hermitage of Hōnen (1133–1212), the monk who founded Jōdo-shū — the Pure Land school — in 1175. His idea was quietly explosive. Japanese Buddhism until then was largely a religion of aristocrats and full-time monks, who pursued enlightenment through study, ritual and hard ascetic practice. Hōnen read the scriptures, concluded that such methods were beyond ordinary people in a corrupt age, and taught instead that salvation came through faith in Amida Buddha and the simple spoken invocation of his name: Namu Amida Butsu.

That is the nembutsu — a phrase that means, roughly, I take refuge in Amida Buddha — and it was a door opened to fishermen, farmers and women who had been told for centuries that they could not get through it. The established temples of Mount Hiei did not enjoy being told their scholarship was a detour, and in 1207, after a scandal involving two of Hōnen's disciples and two court ladies, the retired emperor exiled him and had his hut destroyed.

The temple you are standing in is much later. In 1680 Manmu, the thirty-eighth abbot of Chion-in, the great Pure Land headquarters across town, ordered a nembutsu training hall built on the site where Hōnen's hut had stood, and his disciple Ninchō raised it. Hōnen-in later became independent of the sect, and it stayed small. In the graveyard behind are writers who mattered: Tanizaki Junichirō (1886–1965), whose novel The Makioka Sisters is one of the great books of modern Japan, and the economist Kawakami Hajime (1879–1946), a Kyoto University professor who turned Marxist and died in prison.

The grounds are free and open, roughly 6:00 to 16:00, but the halls are normally shut — the buildings open only for two short windows a year, traditionally in early April and early November, and even those dates shift, so check locally. People come here to pray, not to be toured. Keep it quiet.
stops.entranceFeeNote: Free to enter the grounds. The main halls open only during two short windows a year (traditionally early April and early November), when a conservation contribution of a few hundred yen is asked. Verify the current dates locally.
stops.openingHours: Grounds open daily, roughly 6:00 to 16:00, free. The temple buildings are closed most of the year and open only for brief spring and autumn windows — check before travelling for the interiors.
stops.accessibility: The gate and the main path are level but the paving is uneven, and there are shallow stone steps up to some parts of the grounds. Not step-free throughout.
stops.insiderTip: Do not just photograph the gate and leave — walk through it and stand between the two raked sand mounds, which is the point of them. Then look for the old precept stone beside the gate, forbidding garlic, meat and alcohol beyond that line.
stops.nextStopDirections: Come back down to the Philosopher's Path and turn left, continuing south with the canal. Follow it for roughly fifteen to twenty minutes, past the small cafés, until the path ends near the main road. Cross at the lights and walk up the signed lane opposite — the gate ahead among the maple trees is Eikan-dō.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: Mikel Lizarralde, CC BY-SA 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons

stops.name: Eikan-dō (Zenrin-ji)
stops.narration:
This temple is older than almost everything else you will see today, and its most famous possession is a statue caught in the act of being kind. This is Eikan-dō, formally Zenrin-ji, founded in 853 by Shinshō, a disciple of Kūkai — the monk who established Shingon Buddhism in Japan and is credited, among much else, with the kana syllabary the language is written in. That founding date falls only a few decades after Kyoto became the capital.

Start with the statue, the Mikaeri Amida. It is a standing Amida Buddha, and instead of facing forward it looks back over its left shoulder. The story attached to it is the reason. In 1082 the monk Eikan was leading a group in ritual circumambulation — walking around the image while chanting — when, the legend says, the Buddha stepped down from its dais and joined the procession. Eikan stopped, stunned. The Buddha turned its head and looked back at him and, in some versions of the tale, said: Eikan, you are slow. Ever since, the image has been made looking back, and the pose carries a doctrine in it: Amida does not stride ahead to the Pure Land leaving stragglers behind. He waits for the ones who fall behind. That is the whole promise of the Pure Land school, cast in wood.

The temple switched schools over its long life — founded in the Shingon tradition, later reshaped as a Pure Land centre, and today the head temple of the Seizan branch of Jōdo-shū. That is normal in Japan: institutions survive by being reassigned and repurposed as the political weather changes. What did not change is the setting. Eikan-dō is famous above all for its maples — around three thousand of them, which in late November and early December turn the hillside into a tunnel of red and draw enormous night-illumination crowds. In the week you are walking, the maples are bare and the corridors are nearly empty, which is the point.

Follow the covered wooden walkway that links the buildings — the Garyūrō, the "lying dragon corridor", named for the way it snakes up the slope — and climb to the Tahōtō, the multi-treasure pagoda, for a view back down over the roofs of Kyoto. Along the way you pass the pond garden, and you can look at the Amida from the side and from behind, which is the angle the statue was made for.

Admission is around ¥1,000 for adults, with reduced rates for students and children — the temple raised its regular fees from 1 April 2026, after years unchanged — and hours are roughly 9:00 to 17:00 with the last admission at 16:00. Prices and hours move; verify at the gate, and carry cash. The walkways are wooden and uneven, with steps between levels, so take the hillside slowly.
stops.entranceFeeNote: Around ¥1,000 for adults, with lower rates for university, high-school and younger students, following a fee revision from 1 April 2026. Autumn foliage and night-viewing periods are priced separately. Verify at the gate.
stops.openingHours: Generally 9:00 to 17:00 daily, with last admission at 16:00. Hours and fees change during the autumn exhibition and night-viewing season (roughly November to early December). Confirm on the day.
stops.accessibility: A hillside temple, not step-free. The route climbs through connected wooden corridors and halls with steps and uneven boards, and the view from the pagoda is reached by stairs. Wheelchair access is very limited.
stops.insiderTip: The Mikaeri Amida looks over its shoulder, so walk around to see it from behind — the pose only makes complete sense from the back. Then climb to the Tahōtō pagoda: in winter, with the maples bare, you get the view over Kyoto's roofs that the autumn crowds never see.
stops.nextStopDirections: Leave Eikan-dō and walk south-west, downhill for five to ten minutes, following the signs and the canal branch toward Nanzen-ji. You come out at the top of the temple's main approach; walk down it, and the great Sanmon gate is ahead of you.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: Suicasmo, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

stops.name: Nanzen-ji
stops.narration:
This is the top of the Zen hierarchy in Kyoto, and it began with an emperor playing house. In 1264 the retired emperor Kameyama built himself a detached palace here, in the foothills of the eastern mountains; in 1291 he converted it into a Zen temple and installed a Chinese-trained monk, Mukan Fumon, as founding abbot. That inversion — an emperor's retirement home becoming a monastery where monks sat in meditation — is a very Kyoto move.

Nanzen-ji's rank needs explaining, because it explains the buildings. Japanese Zen had borrowed a Chinese ranking idea, the Gozan — the Five Mountains, a league table of the greatest Zen temples. Under the Ashikaga shoguns it was rewritten so that Nanzen-ji sat above the five, in a rank called Gozan no ue, above the Five Mountains, with the title First Temple of the Land; its abbot supervised the rest. The school is Rinzai Zen, which trains the mind with seated meditation and with kōan — paradoxical questions that logic cannot answer — and which the warrior class adopted because it cultivated a certain hardness.

Ahead of you, the enormous two-storey gate is the Sanmon. The one you see was rebuilt in 1628 by Tōdō Takatora, a powerful lord, as a memorial to the soldiers who died in the 1615 siege of Osaka Castle — the campaign that finished off the last rival house and locked the Tokugawa shoguns into two and a half centuries of power. It is one of the three great temple gates of Japan, and for a fee you can climb it. The staircase inside is genuinely steep, but the balcony sits up in the treetops with the city spread out below. If the view feels theatrical, that is because it is: a famous kabuki play, Sanmon Gosan no Kiri, puts the bandit Ishikawa Goemon on this balcony declaring what a magnificent view it is — a liberty, since Goemon was executed in 1594, thirty-four years before the gate was built.

Beyond the gate, the abbot's quarters, the Hōjō, hold a dry landscape garden — karesansui, where raked gravel and carefully set stones stand in for water and mountains. This one is commonly called the "leaping tiger" garden, and the design is often attributed to Kobori Enshū, the tea master and garden designer of the early Edo period. The name hides a parable: a mother tiger with three cubs must cross a river, one cub being a leopard that would eat the others, and the arrangement of the stones tracks the careful order in which she carries them over. Sit on the veranda and read the stones rather than rush them.

Then walk to the astonishing thing: the Suirokaku, a red-brick aqueduct marching across the temple grounds on tall arches. Built in 1888 as part of the Lake Biwa Canal, it carried water — and still does — from Lake Biwa, over the mountains, into a city that had lost its capital and needed a new economy. That one project gave Kyoto its water supply, its canal-side lanes and Japan's first commercial hydroelectric power. The temple insisted the aqueduct be designed to sit quietly in the grounds; the arches are the compromise, and they have aged into the most photographed thing on the site.

The grounds, the gate seen from below and the aqueduct cost nothing and are open at any hour. Climbing the Sanmon (around ¥600) and entering the Hōjō garden (around ¥600) are ticketed separately, with the buildings open roughly 8:40 to 17:00 and reception closing about twenty minutes early. Verify on the day — hours and the closure of a nearby sub-temple have both changed recently.
stops.entranceFeeNote: The precinct, the aqueduct and the Sanmon seen from below are free. Climbing the Sanmon gate is around ¥600 and the Hōjō garden around ¥600, each sold separately at its own entrance. Verify at the gate.
stops.openingHours: The precinct and the aqueduct are open and free at any hour. The Sanmon gate and the Hōjō garden are open roughly 8:40 to 17:00, with reception closing about twenty minutes before. Confirm on the day — hours and sub-temple closures change.
stops.accessibility: The main precinct is a mix of level gravel and stone paths with some steps. Climbing the Sanmon means a very steep, narrow internal staircase, not advisable for anyone unsteady on their feet. The Hōjō garden is viewed from a level veranda.
stops.insiderTip: The aqueduct is free and open around the clock — walk under the arches and up the path beside it for the classic photograph. And check the imperial gate at the entrance, the Chokushimon: it was moved here from the old imperial palace in 1641 and is opened only when a new abbot is installed.
stops.nextStopDirections: Leave Nanzen-ji by the main approach to the west, cross to the canal side and follow the water north-west for roughly twenty minutes. The route passes the Keage area and then the Okazaki museums; the huge vermilion torii across the road tells you Heian Shrine's grounds are just beyond. It is about a kilometre and a half on foot.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: Te-re, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

stops.name: Heian Shrine
stops.narration:
You finish at the newest thing on the walk, and the most nakedly political. Everything here is Meiji, not medieval. The giant vermilion torii you may have passed on Jingu-michi stands about twenty-four metres high — one of the largest in Japan — and it leads to a shrine built in 1895, not 895. The halls behind it, including the great Daigokuden, are scale replicas, about five-eighths size, of the state halls of the ancient imperial palace.

Why 1895? That year was the 1,100th anniversary of the founding of the capital, and it arrived at a bad moment. The emperor had left for Tokyo in 1868, taking the court and much of the city's reason for existing; Kyoto was haemorrhaging people. So a citizens' organisation raised the money and built a shrine that looked back to the city's imperial golden age — and dressed its own nostalgia in architecture. The shrine enshrines Emperor Kanmu, who moved the capital here in 794, and Emperor Kōmei, the last emperor to reign in Kyoto and the father of the Meiji emperor. Enshrining Kōmei, who died in 1867, was itself a statement about where legitimacy came from.

The city wrapped a festival around it. On 22 October every year the Jidai Matsuri, the Festival of the Ages, sends a procession of around two thousand people in painstaking historical costume from the old imperial palace all the way to this shrine — walking backwards through time, era by era, from the Meiji Restoration to the Enryaku period of 794, when the capital was founded. It is one of Kyoto's three great festivals, alongside the Gion Matsuri and the Aoi Matsuri, and it exists precisely to remind everyone that before Tokyo, there was Kyoto.

The shrine grounds are free, opening at 6:00 and closing around 17:00 in the winter months. The garden behind — the Shin'en, laid out from 1895 by Ogawa Jihei VII, the great Meiji-era landscape designer, using water piped from the same Lake Biwa Canal you saw at Nanzen-ji — is ticketed at around ¥600 for adults and ¥300 for children, and in winter it is open roughly 8:30 to 17:00 with last entry at 16:30. The garden's four sections were added over decades, so it is not one design but a collection, and the stepping stones across the pond are a signature of Ogawa's style. Verify at the gate: the shrine has been repainting parts of the halls, so scaffolding comes and goes.
stops.entranceFeeNote: The shrine grounds, the courtyard and the Otenmon gate are free. The Shin'en garden behind the halls is around ¥600 for adults and ¥300 for children; the garden is free on a couple of days a year. Verify at the gate.
stops.openingHours: Grounds open daily from 6:00, closing around 17:00 from November to mid-February (later in the warmer months). The Shin'en garden opens at 8:30 and in winter closes at 17:00, with last entry at 16:30. Confirm on the day, as hours shift with events and repainting work.
stops.accessibility: The courtyard and the main approach are flat and step-free, with a broad gravel expanse in front of the halls. The garden is a stroll route with gravel paths, stepping stones and some uneven ground — partly accessible, but not step-free throughout.
stops.insiderTip: The garden is the reason to pay here, not the halls: walk all four sections, and look for Ogawa Jihei's stepping stones across the pond, his signature move. If you are here in early April, the weeping cherries over the water are the shrine's show.
stops.nextStopDirections: That is the end of the walk. You are on the edge of the Okazaki museum district: the Kyoto Municipal Museum of Art and the National Museum of Modern Art are a few minutes away, and the Okazaki canal with the Keage Incline — a disused railway once used to haul boats between two levels of the canal — is a short walk north along the water for an easy epilogue. Higashiyama subway station on the Tozai line is a few minutes west of the shrine. Winter dusk comes early, so if you have time to fill, a museum is a warmer bet than another temple.
